clinicalPearls: Ganglia are the commonest soft-tissue swellings of the wrist and hand, consisting of a mucin-filled cyst arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath and connected by a pedicle with a one-way valve mechanism.

The dorsal wrist ganglion classically arises from the scapholunate interval and may be occult, becoming apparent only on wrist flexion or presenting as unexplained dorsal wrist pain before it is palpable.
The volar wrist ganglion typically arises near the radiocarpal or scaphotrapezial joint and lies close to the radial artery, an important consideration before aspiration or excision.
Cysts transilluminate, are usually mobile and may fluctuate in size, often enlarging with activity and regressing with rest.
A significant proportion resolve spontaneously, so reassurance and observation are entirely appropriate for asymptomatic lesions once the diagnosis is confident.
Aspiration is simple but carries a high recurrence rate; surgical excision including the capsular pedicle and stalk offers the lowest recurrence but is not recurrence-free.
Allen test assessment of the radial and ulnar arterial supply is prudent before intervention on a volar ganglion adjacent to the radial artery.
A firm mass that does not transilluminate, is fixed, or lies in an atypical site warrants imaging to exclude other pathology before it is dismissed as a ganglion.
reference.pathophysiology: A ganglion is not a true cyst as it lacks an epithelial lining; instead it is a pseudocyst with a fibrous wall containing viscous mucin rich in hyaluronic acid and other glycosaminoglycans. It is thought to arise from mucoid degeneration of periarticular connective tissue and from capsular or tendon-sheath microtrauma, with a pedicle connecting the cyst to the underlying joint. A hypothesised one-way valve at the stalk allows joint fluid to pass into the cyst but not back, explaining fluctuation in size and the tendency to recur if the stalk is not addressed.
additionalDifferentials: Extensor or flexor tenosynovitis with associated swelling
Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath
Lipoma or other benign soft-tissue tumour
Scapholunate instability causing dorsal wrist pain
Radial artery aneurysm mimicking a volar ganglion
Soft-tissue sarcoma in atypical or rapidly enlarging lesions
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is usually clinical with transillumination of the cyst
Ultrasound to confirm a cystic anechoic lesion and define its relationship to the radial artery
MRI for occult dorsal ganglia presenting as unexplained wrist pain or for atypical solid-feeling masses
Plain radiographs to assess a carpal boss or associated degenerative change
Aspiration demonstrating characteristic clear viscous mucin supports the diagnosis
Allen test to document arterial patency before volar intervention
Histological examination of any excised atypical lesion
redFlags: Solid, fixed or non-transilluminating mass suggesting neoplasm rather than ganglion
Rapid painless enlargement or deep infiltration on imaging
Pulsatile volar swelling raising the possibility of a radial artery aneurysm
Neurological deficit from compression of an adjacent nerve, such as a wrist ganglion involving Guyon canal
reference.prognosis: Benign with an excellent outlook; many resolve without treatment, and although aspiration is frequently followed by recurrence, meticulous surgical excision of the cyst and its stalk achieves durable control in most patients.
pitfalls: Injuring the radial artery during aspiration or excision of a volar wrist ganglion
Incompletely excising the capsular stalk, leading to recurrence
Labelling an occult dorsal ganglion as functional wrist pain and missing the diagnosis
Assuming every wrist swelling is a ganglion and overlooking a soft-tissue sarcoma or arterial aneurysm
Failing to counsel patients that recurrence and spontaneous resolution are both common
references: British Society for Surgery of the Hand guidance on ganglia
